cap: The world used 102.3 Mt of hydrogen in 2025. Only 0.88 Mt, less than 1%, was made with low emissions.
Demand keeps growing in industry and refining. Switch to production: natural gas and coal still make almost all of it.
What grew fastest in 2025: installed electrolysis more than doubled, and investment rose by about 70%.
China holds 64% of the world's electrolysers, and only 16% of the 2030 pipeline is running or has a final investment decision.
The world map shows how exposed each country is. Urea: Brazil imports all it uses, 40% of it from the Middle East.
Switch the lens to ammonia, or search any country in the top bar: Morocco and South Korea import all of their ammonia.
Progress to 2030 targets: committed projects cover only a small share of most national goals.
From announcement to reality: 27.9 Mt is announced for 2030, but only 4.4 Mt is committed and 1.1 Mt is operating.
The electrolyser race: China leads with 2.7 GW. Press 2026 and Europe jumps to about 2.7 GW with projects already financed.
Factories can build 58 GW of electrolysers a year, more than six times what projects need.
Where the 2030 projects are: Europe leads, and Latin America, with 4.4 Mt announced, is one of the largest renewable pipelines.
The cost gap: renewable hydrogen still costs from over USD 3/kg to beyond USD 10/kg, against about USD 1 to 4 for natural gas.
Investment in low-emissions plants reached about USD 6.65 billion in 2025, and 66 countries now have a hydrogen strategy.
Brazil in focus: the largest urea importer in the world, with USD 58 billion in Nova Indústria Brasil and 44 renewable hydrogen projects selected.
